newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan reassures Gore on U.S. troop levels.
newsitem.headline: Japan reassures Gore on U.S. troop levels.

text.p: Vice President Al Gore, reassured by Japanese officials that there was no threat to the future of U.S. troops in Japan, heads for China on Monday to push forward relations with the region's fast emerging superpower.
Gore wraps up his mainly symbolic Japanese visit with a meeting with Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and a speech at an environmental conference, a subject dear to the vice president.

Although the main focus of Gore's trip to east Asia is the four days he spends in China, his talks with Japanese officials cleared away any lingering worries about the future of "Aircraft Japan" as the United States' main military base in Asia.

"The Japanese government feels that the U.S. military is an important factor for stability in the region," Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda told Gore shortly after the vice president arrived in Tokyo on Sunday. "Now is not the time to start discussions on reducing U.S. troops."

Local authorities on Okinawa, where about half of the 47,000 U.S. troops in Japan are stationed, want the bases closed by 2015, an action Tokyo strongly opposes. The 47,000 troops make up half of the U.S. forces in Asia.
Prime Minister Hashimoto chose the day Gore arrived to announce he planned to push through parliament a new law to seek continued leases on private land used by U.S. bases on Okinawa.
Gore was equally adamant that Washington did not want changes in troop levels in Japan.
Asked if the current force can be reduced over the next decade, Gore replied: "I think we need them now and for the foreseeable future.
"In my view, this would be the worst time to have some reduction in U.S. forces here," Gore said.
In an arrival statement on Sunday, Gore said his visit was to reaffirm America's commitment to the region.
"The security and prosperity of the United States is vitally tied to the Asia-Pacific region," Gore said.
Both the United States and Japan agree that China is the key to peace in Asia and hope to draw Beijing into dialogue on all issues involving the region.

Gore set off from the United States upbeat about the chances for improving relations with China, which has frequently clashed with Washington in recent years, particularly over trade, Taiwan and human rights.

"Change is taking place rapidly inside China...The growth of the free sector of their economy is far outstripping the growth in the state-owned sector," he told reporters on his plane before arriving in Japan.

"Both our countries are clearly signalling to one another that we want to find a way to move forward in the relationship," said Gore, who planned to discuss a broad range of issues, including the environment and the future of Hong Kong.

Gore said he would "touch on every issue that has a particular impact for our two countries" -- including charges Beijing tried to funnel money to influence last year's presidential elections and some congressional races.

Gore will be the highest-ranking U.S. official to visit China since President George Bush's trip there in 1989 -- shortly before Chinese troops brutally ended pro-democracy demonstrations in Tiananmen Square.

Part of his discussions will deal with preparations for an exchange of visits by U.S. President Bill Clinton and and his Chinese counterpart Jiang Zemin. The Chinese leader is expected to visit the United States late this year and Clinton tentatively plans to go to China in 1998.
